claim.why_it_matters: Indentation is the only thing binding a sub-item to its parent rule in 13.18.57.4, and here it is the only thing lost. Flattened, page 528 shows two different 'g)' items at the same level as '7)' - one belonging to General rule 6) (carried over from page 527) and one belonging to 7) - so a reader or a tool walking the list cannot tell which rule either 'g)' qualifies, and '1.' through '4.' read as top-level enumerations instead of the four sub-cases of 7) d) (upper limit for a body group when some control heading carries OR PAGE). The transcription preserves this nesting correctly on pages 527, 529 and 535 of the same clause, which confirms page 528 is drift, not house style.

verdict.reasoning: CONFIRMED by independent inspection of both sources. (1) PDF render (E:/Temp/specrecon/v528/spec_p528.png, printed folio 498) shows three clearly distinct left margins: the '7)' marker sits at the outermost rule indent; the 'a)'..'g)' markers sit one level in; the '1.'..'4.' markers sit a further level in under d). The unmarked continuation paragraph 'If a report footing is defined and is not on a page by itself...' is set at the body-text indent of the lettered items (aligned with the prose after 'g)'), i.e. it hangs off General rule 6) f) carried over from page 527 - exactly as the claim describes. (2) The markdown (specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines 22212-22238) has every one of those 13 lines at leading-indent 0, verified by measuring the first non-space column of each line. The six quoted strings in the claim match the file verbatim; neither source is misquoted. (3) This is NOT house style, and the proof is internal to the same enumeration rather than merely adjacent-page: the transcription's convention is 0 / 3 / 6 spaces for rule / letter / numeral levels, and page 527 (lines 22174-22202, the SAME clause 13.18.57.4 and the SAME General rule 6)) follows it exactly - a) through f) at indent 3, their 1./2. sub-items at indent 6. General rule 6)'s enumeration is therefore transcribed with items a)-f) at indent 3 on page 527 and its item g) at indent 0 on page 528: one list, split by the page break, rendered at two different levels. Page 529 (lines 22250-22262, still 13.18.57.4) likewise puts 8) a)-g) at indent 3. So page 528 is a per-page transcription regression. (4) It changes meaning, not just formatting: no prose is missing or reflowed, but the parent binding of every sub-item on the page is destroyed. As transcribed the document asserts two sibling 'g)' items straddling a '7)' at the same level, and presents '1.'-'4.' - the four OR-PAGE body-group upper-limit cases that are normatively scoped to 7) d) - as top-level enumerations. Rule scope is normative content, so this is correctly classified structural rather than cosmetic.
verdict.corrected_description: Real and essentially as described; one supporting citation in the claim is wrong. Page 528 flattens all of 13.18.57.4's nesting to column 0: the tail continuation of General rule 6) f), item 6) g), rule 7), the seven lettered sub-items a)-g) under 7), and the four numbered sub-cases 1.-4. under 7) d) are all at indent 0, where the transcription's own convention (and the PDF's typography) is 0 / 3 / 6 spaces for the rule / letter / numeral levels. The claim cites pages 527, 529 and 535 as same-clause counterexamples; only 527 and 529 are in clause 13.18.57.4 - page 535 is clause 13.18.60 (USAGE) and merely corroborates the house style. The strongest evidence, which the claim understates, is that General rule 6)'s own lettered enumeration is transcribed at indent 3 on page 527 (a through f) and indent 0 on page 528 (g), so a single list is split across the page break at two different levels - unambiguous per-page drift. Fix is indentation only: no text is missing, misquoted, or reworded on this page.
